opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few things that really matter, and some of them are a bit different from what you'd look for in a typical research manager.

The first is that they need to genuinely care about the problem. Alignment isn't a field where you can just optimize for papers or for looking productive. We're trying to figure out how to make systems that are much smarter than us reliably do what we want, and that's a hard problem where it's easy to fool yourself. So I want someone who is motivated by actually solving it, and who will keep asking, "Is this really moving us toward a solution, or does it just feel like progress?"

The second is strong research taste, or at least the ability to recognize it. A research manager doesn't have to be the best individual researcher on the team, but they need to tell the difference between a promising direction and a dead end, and help people prioritize. A lot of the value of a manager comes from helping the team say no to things: cutting projects that aren't working and doubling down on the ones that are.

Third, they need to be good with people. That sounds obvious, but in practice it means helping researchers grow, giving honest feedback, unblocking people, and creating an environment where people feel comfortable saying "I think this approach is wrong," even to someone senior. Alignment research benefits a lot from people disagreeing openly, because we don't have a well-established paradigm yet.

And fourth, I'd want someone comfortable with the empirical, engineering-heavy side of the work. A lot of what we do now involves working with large models directly: training them, running experiments, building evaluations. So it helps a lot if a manager has hands-on machine learning experience and understands what it actually takes to get an experiment working at scale.

If I had to boil it down: someone who cares deeply about getting alignment right, has good judgment about what's worth working on, and can make the people around them more effective. That combination is rarer than you'd hope, and it's really valuable.

r001.rationale: The response lists research judgment and people management as useful traits, but does not suggest they may be anticorrelated.

r002.rationale: It describes what one research manager should do; it does not propose separate research lead and management roles.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss coordination or alignment between a research lead and a manager.

r004.rationale: It says a manager should care deeply about alignment, but does not compare that as a hiring filter with any particular career background.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because honestly I think research management is one of the most undervalued roles in the whole field. Everyone wants to be the person who has the brilliant idea, but a lot of what makes a research team actually work is someone who can take a fuzzy, ambitious goal like "figure out how to align systems smarter than us" and turn it into a sequence of concrete projects that people can make progress on week to week.

So the first thing I look for is that they can do that translation. They need to understand the research well enough to know what's a real bottleneck versus what just looks shiny, and to have taste about which experiments will actually tell us something. That doesn't mean they need to be the best researcher in the room. Often they shouldn't be. But they need enough depth that researchers respect their judgement and they can push back when something is drifting.

The second thing is that they genuinely care about the people. A lot of alignment research is high-variance and kind of emotionally taxing. You can spend months on something and it doesn't pan out, or you get scooped, or the problem turns out to be harder than you thought. A good manager notices when someone is stuck or burning out, helps them reframe, and makes sure people get credit and feel like their work matters. In my experience, the teams that do well over multiple years are the ones where people actually want to stay.

And then third, they need to be comfortable with the fact that this is a field where we don't fully know what we're doing yet. We're not building a product with a well-understood spec. The manager has to be okay saying "we're not sure this approach works, here's how we'll find out, and here's what we'll do if it doesn't." People who need certainty or who optimise too hard for looking productive tend to struggle, because they'll steer the team toward safe incremental stuff instead of the uncomfortable questions that actually matter.

If I'm being really honest, the thing that's hard to screen for but matters most is just: do they care about the mission? Alignment work at a frontier lab involves a lot of friction. You're sometimes the people saying "wait, slow down" in an organisation that's moving fast. A manager who deeply believes this matters will fight the right battles and know which ones to let go. Someone who is there because it's an interesting job will, over time, get pulled toward whatever is easiest.

r001.rationale: The response says a manager need not be the best researcher, but it does not suggest research ability and management ability may be negatively related.

r002.rationale: It describes what a manager should do but does not identify separating research leadership and management into distinct roles as a team structure.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss coordination or close alignment between a research lead and a manager.

r004.rationale: It calls mission commitment especially important, but does not compare that hiring filter with a particular career background.

astra-6.text:
I think the most important thing is good research taste: can you identify which problems are actually important for alignment, and which of those we can make progress on empirically today? There are lots of things you could work on that are interesting, but it’s harder to find work that will really help us align much more capable systems.

And then you need to be good at helping other researchers succeed. That means understanding what they’re trying to do, giving useful feedback, and helping them get unstuck, while leaving them enough space to pursue their own ideas. You don’t want every research decision to have to go through the manager.

There’s also a judgment call around when to keep pushing on an idea and when to move on. Research is uncertain, so you need someone who can make those calls without pretending they know how everything will turn out, and who makes it easy for people to disagree with them.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the most important thing is good research taste: being able to identify which questions matter for alignment, and then turn those into projects where you can actually learn something. There’s a lot of uncertainty about what will work, so you want someone who can make progress without pretending that we already know the whole plan.

And then you need someone who’s good at helping other researchers succeed. That means understanding what they’re trying to do, giving useful feedback, and knowing when to get involved and when to give them space. Being a really strong researcher yourself doesn’t automatically make you good at that.

I’d also look for someone who can have honest conversations about whether the work is actually helping. It’s easy to pursue something because it’s interesting or because you’re making measurable progress. The harder question is: if this project succeeds, how does that make powerful AI systems safer?
